864.t: Jobs before Preservation Hall: society and fraternity dances
864.s: The orchestra played private and public dances, mostly for white audiences, including fraternity houses uptown.
864.q: Well, we were just spotting around. I mean, we didn't have nothing for him. We didn't have to spotting around, catch him sometimes private forters and sometimes, you know, public dancers. It's just a occasion, nothing for him. We wasn't on nothing for him.

241.t: Playing Speck's dances: Jitney dances, Shark Bay and the twelve-by-twelve room
241.s: He plays jitney dances and then Speck's early dances in a tiny grocery in Marrero with a three-piece band, alternating white and colored nights.
241.q: I didn't know that. Yeah, we first, Specs taught giving dance, by the Zalmo, then, then he went to, uh, Shark Bay, they call it. That's a French. That's French.

403.s: Most people danced; Jones listened rather than danced. Admission was twenty-five to forty cents.
403.q: I wasn't dancing on the couch to see the people going to the dance. Oh yeah.

875.t: Why Black audiences would not pay to dance
875.s: A short exchange on what went on in the back and why dime dances would not work for Black patrons.
875.q: Yeah. But for our people, man, no, they don't go for that. They don't go for no ten cents to dance, man. No. Ain't gonna play. I see. You were talking more about the Sam Morgan or Isaiah Morgan bands.

296.t: Calico balls, admission prices and dance band size
296.s: Calico balls, 25-cent admission, and ten-man bands usually without drums or piano.
296.q: Did they use a piano? They said, well, 10 men use this as good.

300.t: Reel two begins and a record by Lee Collins and Joe Robichaux
300.s: Allen marks reel two and plays records; Humphrey recalls jitney dance playing that went on all night for two years.
300.q: Man, they'd pick up, see, see, uh, them jet, those jet, those jetty dances. Mm-hmm. Well, you know, you get one round off a chorus. Mm-hmm. Gals that dance around there, take the ticket out your hand. Mm-hmm. It start off, just all these playin' on that. Mm-hmm. When they end up playin' just that…

309.t: Dance halls, the five-minute slow drag and dime dances
309.s: He explains the dance-hall pricing at the Music Box, Budweiser and Levita, and the popular five-minute slow drag.
309.ch: Early music and bands on the coast
309.q: Well, I'll tell you, uh, you see playing the blues at that time, it was mostly slow numbers, you know, and, uh, they could tell more about you playing the blues than they could by you playing any other numbers because the blues was always slow. And just like when I started playing at the, uh,…

333.s: He explains jitney dances, cheap dances where tickets bought dances with girls.
333.q: Jitney dances. Oh, well a jitney dance was like a lot of people came in at a low price, you know what I mean? We used to have, there were certain nights that they would have like fifteen, twenty cents, and you could hear Benny Carter, you could hear Fletcher Henderson, for twenty-five, they were…

9.t: How hostesses and tickets worked at big ballrooms
9.s: At big ballrooms patrons paid admission and bought tickets for hostesses, and bands alternated half-hour sets.
9.ch: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
9.q: Well, they had girls, too -- hostesses. The big-time ballrooms, they had hostesses. You know, like the Savoy, the Roseland -- they had hostesses. And the Arcadia, yeah.

94.t: The La Vida Ballroom, dime-a-dance, and the drummer who slept
94.s: He explains ten-cent dancing at the La Vida and the drummer who played steady tempo while sleeping.
94.q: Yes, Celestin played mostly for ballrooms, colleges. Kid Rene' played this place called the La Vida Ballroom, it was 10¢ a dance place.
